questions.q: Why were the economic reforms of 1991 introduced, and what did liberalisation involve?

answer.text: By 1991 India faced a severe economic crisis. Years of heavy government spending had produced large deficits, foreign exchange reserves fell so low that they could cover only a few weeks of imports, prices were rising sharply, and the country was deep in debt. Unable to meet its payments, India borrowed from the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, which required it to reform its economy. This led to the New Economic Policy of 1991.

Liberalisation meant removing the many controls and restrictions that had bound the economy. Industrial licensing was abolished for most industries, restrictions on private investment were eased, the financial sector was reformed, taxes were rationalised, and trade was opened up by lowering tariffs and welcoming foreign investment.

answer: These measures aimed to make the economy more efficient, competitive and open to the world.

questions.q: Assess the impact of the 1991 economic reforms on India.
answer: The reforms of 1991, involving liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, had far-reaching and mixed effects.

answer.text: The reforms lifted India's rate of economic growth and made it one of the fast-growing economies. The service sector, especially information technology and business outsourcing, expanded rapidly. Foreign investment and foreign exchange reserves rose sharply, inflation was brought under control, and consumers gained a wider choice of goods.

However, growth did not create enough jobs, a problem called jobless growth. Agriculture was neglected and its growth slowed, hurting the large rural population. The benefits of reform were unevenly shared, and economic inequality increased, while small domestic producers faced tough foreign competition.

answer: Thus the reforms brought faster growth and modernisation, but their gains did not reach all sections equally.
